questions.prompt: Why is the program counter important in a stored-program computer?
questions.answer: It tracks the address of the next instruction to fetch.
options: There is not enough information to determine the result.
It tracks the address of the next instruction to fetch.
It tracks the address of the previous instruction to fetch.

blocks.title: Key vocabulary
items: LMC — Educational model of a stored-program accumulator computer.
accumulator — Register holding current working data and arithmetic results.
program counter — Register holding address of the next instruction to fetch.
mnemonic — Symbolic name representing a machine instruction.

blocks.title: Mailboxes
blocks.text: Instructions and numeric data occupy addressed memory mailboxes. DAT reserves a data location. Programs execute the instructions addressed by the program counter.

blocks.title: Accumulator and PC
blocks.text: INP reads into ACC; LDA reads memory into ACC; STA writes ACC to memory. The PC normally advances after a fetch, unless a branch selects a new address.

blocks.title: Branches and stopping
blocks.text: ADD and SUB update ACC; OUT prints ACC; BRA always branches; BRZ tests for zero; BRP tests a non-negative result in standard LMC; HLT ends the program.

blocks.title: Worked example · Track each change
blocks.text: 00 INP: ACC = 7. 01 STA 10: mailbox 10 becomes 7; ACC remains 7. 02 LDA 10: ACC = 7. 03 ADD 10: ACC = 14. 04 OUT: output is 14. 05 HLT: stop. Data mailbox 10 is separate from instruction addresses 00–05.

blocks.title: Predict the registers
blocks.text: What are ACC and mailbox 20 after the first two instructions?

blocks.title: Calculate ACC
blocks.text: Follow LDA 20 and SUB 21. Use the stored value 9 and constant 4.

blocks.title: Completed trace
blocks.text: INP sets ACC to 9. STA 20 saves 9. LDA 20 reloads it. SUB 21 subtracts 4, leaving ACC = 5. OUT prints 5; HLT stops.
